title: Incidents, PSIRF and learning from harm
blurb: Recognise and report near misses, incidents and Never Events, and explain how PSIRF and LFPSE turn them into learning.
question: A nurse draws up a medicine for the wrong patient but notices before giving it. No harm occurs. What should she do about the event?

teach.body: A patient safety incident is something unintended or unexpected in healthcare that could have harmed, or did harm, one or more patients. A near miss is an event that could have caused harm but did not, because it was caught in time or by chance. In plain English: anything that went wrong, or nearly went wrong, is worth recording, because the same weakness may hurt the next patient. Recording events whether or not they cause harm gives vital insight into what can go wrong and why.

teach.h: After an incident or near miss
teach.caption: Near misses are recorded too, even though no one was harmed.
PSIRF is a contractual requirement under the NHS Standard Contract, including acute, ambulance, mental health, community and maternity services.

head: Aim
What it means on the ward
rows: Involve patients, families and staff affected
Look at how the system let it happen
Match the response to the learning needed
Strengthen the response system, not blame

teach.h: Key dates in the reporting landscape

items.label: Never Events framework and list (still active)
NRLS closed; LFPSE is the national service

teach.body: Never Events are patient safety incidents that are wholly preventable because guidance or safety recommendations providing strong systemic protective barriers are available nationally and should have been implemented by all providers. Examples include wrong site surgery and a misplaced nasogastric tube that is used. The 2018 framework and list (updated 2021) remain active while a replacement is developed; they are recorded under the Never Event category on LFPSE, with learning responses under PSIRF.
teach.cite: NHS England Never Events policy and framework

teach.h: Complaints and feedback are learning too
teach.body: Code 24.1: never allow someone's complaint to affect the care that is provided. Code 24.2: use all complaints as a form of feedback and an opportunity for reflection and learning to improve practice. Respond calmly, listen, apologise where appropriate, deal with any immediate need and explain how to make a formal complaint. Proficiency P6.9 asks nurses to work with people, families and colleagues on improvement, sharing feedback and learning.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Staff Nurse Ola on an orthopaedic ward
teach.body: Ola prepares Mr Grant's evening antibiotic but, on the bedside identity check, realises it was prescribed for Mr Green in the next bed. Nothing is given. She records the near miss on the trust's reporting system, which feeds LFPSE, and tells the nurse in charge. At the safety huddle the team notes the similar names and side-by-side beds; they move one patient and add a name alert. No one is blamed: the learning is about the system.

teach.text: The NRLS no longer exists: it closed on 30 June 2024 and LFPSE replaced it. And PSIRF replaced the Serious Incident Framework (2015). Old names in an option are a sign it is out of date.

items: Record incidents and near misses, harm or no harm, on the local system that feeds LFPSE.
PSIRF aims: compassionate engagement, system-based learning, proportionate responses, supportive oversight.
Never Events: wholly preventable because strong national barriers exist; recorded as such on LFPSE.
Be open with the person (Code 14) and, for notifiable incidents, the provider follows reg 20.
Complaints must not affect care (Code 24.1) and are feedback for learning (24.2).

summary: You can now recognise and report incidents, near misses and Never Events, and explain how PSIRF and the LFPSE service support learning rather than blame. You can also respond to complaints and involve people and families in improvement.

A.q: A nurse realises she has drawn up insulin for the wrong patient and stops before giving it. What should she do about the event?
options: Record it as a near miss on the trust's own system
Tell the nurse in charge, with no written report needed
Discard the dose and note it in her reflective diary
Report it to the NMC as a fitness to practise matter
A.why: Near misses are patient safety events and are recorded so the system can learn, whether or not harm occurred. Local systems feed the national LFPSE service (NHS England; Code 19.1).

whyNot.1: Telling the nurse in charge is good, but the event should also be recorded so learning is captured.
whyNot.2: A private diary entry does not allow the organisation to learn from the event.
whyNot.3: An honest near miss is a learning matter, not a fitness to practise referral.

A.q: Which national NHS service now records and analyses patient safety events in England?
options: The National Reporting and Learning System (NRLS)
The Yellow Card scheme run by the MHRA
The Serious Incident Framework database
The Learn from Patient Safety Events service
A.why: LFPSE is the national NHS system for recording and analysing patient safety events. It replaced the NRLS, which was decommissioned on 30 June 2024 (NHS England).

whyNot.0: The NRLS was decommissioned on 30 June 2024.
whyNot.1: Yellow Card is for suspected adverse drug reactions and device problems, not general safety events.
whyNot.2: The Serious Incident Framework was replaced by PSIRF and was not a reporting database.

A.q: The Patient Safety Incident Response Framework (PSIRF) replaced which earlier framework?
options: The NHS Standard Contract for providers
The Serious Incident Framework (2015)
The NHS Patient Safety Strategy
The duty of candour regulations
A.why: PSIRF replaced the Serious Incident Framework (2015), with transition expected to be complete by autumn 2023 (NHS England).

whyNot.0: PSIRF is a contractual requirement under the NHS Standard Contract; it did not replace it.
whyNot.2: PSIRF is a key part of the NHS Patient Safety Strategy; it did not replace it.
whyNot.3: Regulation 20 (duty of candour) remains in force alongside PSIRF.

B.q: Which of these is one of the four aims of PSIRF?
options: Identifying the individual staff member at fault
A full investigation of every incident
Reporting all incidents to the CQC
Compassionate engagement of those affected
B.why: PSIRF's four aims are compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected; system-based approaches to learning; considered and proportionate responses; and supportive oversight (NHS England).

whyNot.0: PSIRF focuses on how incidents happen in the system, not on attributing blame.
whyNot.1: PSIRF calls for considered and proportionate responses, not a uniform full investigation.
whyNot.2: Events are recorded through LFPSE-compliant systems; CQC notification is a separate duty for specific events.

B.q: What makes a patient safety incident a Never Event?
options: It caused the death of a patient in hospital
It was reported to the coroner after harm
It is wholly preventable through national barriers
It happened more than once in the same trust in a year
B.why: Never Events are defined as wholly preventable because guidance or safety recommendations providing strong systemic protective barriers are available nationally and should have been implemented by all providers (NHS England, 2018 framework).

whyNot.0: A Never Event need not cause death; the definition is about preventability through national barriers.
whyNot.1: Coroner involvement does not define a Never Event.
whyNot.3: Repetition does not define a Never Event; one occurrence qualifies.

B.q: Mrs Ahmed tells the nurse she is making a formal complaint because her call bell was not answered quickly. She now needs help to the toilet. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask a colleague to help her as the complaint involves him
Help her now and explain how to make her complaint
Ask her to wait while he informs the ward manager
Tell her the delay was due to an emergency elsewhere
B.why: Code 24.1: never let a complaint affect the care provided. Meeting her immediate need, listening and explaining the complaints process is the compassionate, open response (Code 24.2 use complaints as feedback).

whyNot.0: Handing over care because of a complaint risks letting the complaint affect her care.
whyNot.2: Making her wait to escalate delays care she needs now.
whyNot.3: Giving an excuse before listening is defensive and does not address her concern.

C.q: Mr Lowe's observations were not done for 10 hours overnight. He deteriorated and was transferred to ICU. What does regulation 20 require of the hospital?
options: Tell him in person promptly with an apology, then in writing
Tell him in writing within 28 days of the incident
Wait for the investigation report before telling him anything
Record it internally, as candour applies to severe harm
C.why: Transfer to ICU is a moderate increase in treatment, so this is moderate harm and a notifiable safety incident. Reg 20 requires notification in person as soon as reasonably practicable, with an apology, followed by written notification and records (Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014).

whyNot.1: Notification must be in person as soon as reasonably practicable; 28 days relates to prolonged psychological harm.
whyNot.2: The person should be told what is known without waiting for the investigation.
whyNot.3: Moderate harm, including transfer to ICU, is notifiable, not only severe harm.

C.q: After a patient falls and fractures her hip, a colleague says the review should identify which nurse failed to check on her. Which response best reflects PSIRF?
options: Agree, as the nurse responsible must be identified first
Suggest referring the nurse on duty to the NMC straight away
Explain the review looks at system factors, to learn
Suggest closing the case, as falls are not investigated
C.why: PSIRF uses system-based approaches to learning, focusing on how incidents happen and the factors that contribute, rather than attributing blame. Responses are proportionate and involve those affected (NHS England).

whyNot.0: PSIRF moves away from attributing blame towards understanding contributory factors.
whyNot.1: An NMC referral is not the starting point for learning from an incident.
whyNot.3: Falls with harm are patient safety incidents that need a proportionate learning response.

C.q: A nasogastric tube was used for feeding without a position check and was found in the lung. How should this be recorded?
options: On the NRLS, followed by a Serious Incident Framework investigation
As a Never Event on LFPSE, with a PSIRF learning response
As a near miss, because the tube was found before discharge
As a RIDDOR dangerous occurrence reported to the HSE
C.why: A misplaced NG tube that is used is on the Never Events list. Never Events are recorded under the Never Event category on LFPSE, with learning responses in line with PSIRF (NHS England).

whyNot.0: The NRLS closed in June 2024 and PSIRF replaced the Serious Incident Framework.
whyNot.2: The patient was fed through a misplaced tube, so this is an incident, not a near miss.
whyNot.3: RIDDOR covers specified workplace events; patient safety incidents go through LFPSE.

reteach.title: Black box thinking
reteach.question: Why do airlines want pilots to report every near miss, and how does that apply to a ward?

blocks.body: Aviation learns because crews report near misses without fear, and the data is used to redesign systems. PSIRF brings the same idea to the NHS: record events, harm or not, through LFPSE, involve the people affected, and ask how the system made the error easy. Blaming the last person to touch the problem leaves the trap in place for the next nurse.

blocks.text: No harm does not mean no report. Near misses are the cheapest lessons the system will ever get.

explain.body: Record incidents and near misses on the organisation's system, which feeds LFPSE. Honest reporting is how the system finds weaknesses before someone is harmed.

test.q: A healthcare assistant almost hoisted a patient with the wrong sling size but noticed in time. What should happen?
options: No further action, as no harm occurred
The assistant writes a formal apology
The sling is reported to the HSE
The event is recorded as a near miss
test.why: Near misses are recorded so learning can prevent future harm (NHS England LFPSE; Code 19.1).

whyNot.0: No harm does not remove the value of recording the event.
whyNot.1: There is no patient harm requiring a formal written apology; the event needs recording.
whyNot.2: A near miss with the wrong sling size is not a RIDDOR report to the HSE.

explain.body: PSIRF replaced the Serious Incident Framework (2015). It has four aims: compassionate engagement, system-based learning, considered and proportionate responses, and supportive oversight.

test.q: Under PSIRF, how should a trust choose its response to an incident?
options: Match the response to the learning needed
Investigate every incident in the same way
Investigate incidents that caused death
Let the staff involved choose the response
test.why: PSIRF calls for considered and proportionate responses: the type of learning response depends on what can be learnt (NHS England).

whyNot.1: A uniform approach is what PSIRF moved away from.
whyNot.2: Responses are not limited to deaths; any incident may merit a learning response.
whyNot.3: Staff are involved, but responses are planned by the organisation with oversight.

explain.body: LFPSE replaced the NRLS on 30 June 2024. Never Events (wholly preventable because national barriers exist) are recorded under the Never Event category on LFPSE.

test.q: When was the National Reporting and Learning System decommissioned?
options: 31 March 2023
30 June 2024
1 April 2025
1 July 2022
test.why: The NRLS was decommissioned on 30 June 2024; organisations now record on LFPSE through compliant local systems (NHS England).

whyNot.0: March 2023 is before the NRLS was decommissioned.
whyNot.2: April 2025 is after the decommissioning date.
whyNot.3: 1 July 2022 is when integrated care systems were legally established, not the NRLS closure.

explain.body: Never let a complaint affect care (Code 24.1); treat it as feedback and a chance to reflect and improve (Code 24.2). Listen, apologise where appropriate, meet immediate needs and explain the complaints process.

test.q: According to the Code, how should nurses treat complaints?
options: As feedback and an opportunity to learn
As matters for the complaints team to handle
As reasons to transfer the person's care
As grounds to restrict family visiting
test.why: Code 24.2: use all complaints as a form of feedback and an opportunity for reflection and learning to improve practice.

whyNot.1: The complaints team handles formal processes, but every registrant should use complaints as feedback.
whyNot.2: Transferring care because of a complaint risks letting it affect care (Code 24.1).
whyNot.3: Restricting visiting in response to a complaint would be punitive.
